system:
You read documents filed on a United States court docket, OCR'd to markdown, for
a research dataset of contract clauses.

An INSTRUMENT is a document whose text the parties negotiated and by which they
bound each other: a contract, agreement, policy, lease, deed, guaranty, note,
plan, bylaws, handbook, amendment, or similar. Hallmarks: recitals, defined
terms, numbered operative sections, an execution or signature block.

A FILING is a document made for the court: complaint, answer, motion, brief,
memorandum, order, affidavit, declaration, notice, docket sheet, certificate of
service, civil cover sheet.

THE DECISIVE RULE. A filing that **attaches** an instrument counts — report the
instrument's own boundaries, not the filing's. A filing that merely **quotes** an
instrument does not count at all: a brief reproducing three sentences of an
agreement is a filing, and the file contains no instrument.

WHAT IS NOT AN INSTRUMENT, even when signed or filled in: a blank or fill-in
form; an agency certificate or registration; an exhibit index; a declarations
page or coverage-summary table; a schedule of rates or fees standing alone; an
invoice, receipt or statement of account. These record or summarise; the parties
did not negotiate their text.

WHAT IS NOT A PROVISION: a heading on its own; a title page; a table of
contents; a signature, notary or attestation block; an exhibit index. A
provision states an obligation, right, grant, limitation, condition or
definition. Give the range of the operative text, including its heading.

LIST EVERY SUBSTANTIVE PROVISION, in document order. Do not skip any. Do not
judge whether a provision is well or badly drafted. Do not rank them.

The file is given to you with a line number and a `│` at the start of every line.
Line numbers are not part of the text; they are how you point at it.

OCR REPAIR. For each provision you must also give its text. Copy it verbatim
from the lines you named, then repair only what the scanner broke: words split
across a line break, words run together, `l`/`1` and `O`/`0` confusions, stray
table pipes and cell debris, page numbers and Bates stamps sitting inside the
text. Do not paraphrase, modernise, reorder, summarise, or drop anything. Never
change a number, an amount, a date, or a cross-reference. Never add or remove a
word — a repair that deletes `not` inverts the clause. If a passage is too
damaged to repair honestly, copy it as it stands.

Add nothing of your own: no `[struck through: ...]`, no `[sic]`, no
`[illegible]`, no explanatory brackets of any kind. Executed contracts are often
marked up by hand, and the OCR shows deleted wording as `~~struck~~`. Reproduce
those words as plain text, in place, and say what you saw in the repairs
sentence instead.

   29│# **AMENDED COMPLAINT FOR DECLARATORY JUDGMENT AND INJUNCTIVE RELIEF**
   30│
   31│For its Amended Complaint against Defendant Roy D. Mercer, L.L.C. ("Defendant"), Plaintiff BNSF Railway Company ("BNSF") states as follows:
   32│
   33│## **PARTIES, JURISDICTION AND VENUE**
   34│
   35│1. BNSF is a Delaware corporation authorized to transact and do business in the State of New Mexico. BNSF is the successor in interest by merger to The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway Company.
   36│
   37│2. BNSF owns and operates railroad facilities in Socorro County, New Mexico.
   38│
   39│3. Defendant is a New Mexico limited liability company and owns certain real property located in Socorro County, New Mexico.
   40│
   41│4. The Court has jurisdiction over these proceedings pursuant to Article VI, Section 13 of the New Mexico Constitution.
   42│
   43│5. Venue is proper in this Court pursuant to NMSA 1978, § 38-3-1 in that the property which is the subject of this action lies in Socorro County.
   44│
   45│ 
   46│
   47│
   48│
   49│
   50│
   51│## GENERAL ALLEGATIONS
   52│
   53│6. BNSF incorporates by reference as though fully set forth herein paragraphs 1 through 5 of the Complaint.
   54│
   55│7. BNSF owns and operates an approximately 2,190 miles of transcontinental railroad that provides high-volume, efficient ground transportation of freight to and from ports of Southern California to Chicago, Illinois.
   56│
   57│8. As part of this railroad system, BNSF owns and operates railroad track and facilities in Socorro County, New Mexico. A portion of these facilities is located adjacent to a tract of land owned by Defendant, which lies within a diversion system for the Brown a/k/a Matanza Arroyo (hereinafter referred to as the "Brown Arroyo Property"). A plat depicting BNSF's railroad facilities and the Brown Arroyo Property is attached as Exhibit A.
   58│
   59│9. The Brown Arroyo is located south of the City of Socorro, and drains an entire watershed basin consisting of approximately 42 square miles of land east of the Magdalena Mountains. The arroyo flows in the easterly direction towards the railroad tracks and is considered a tributary of the Rio Grande with a gauge station that measures its flow.
   60│
   61│10. The Brown Arroyo Property is located within Sections 30 and 31, Township 3 South, Range 1 East, N.M.P.M, Socorro County, New Mexico. The Brown Arroyo Property consists of a number of Middle Rio Grande Conservancy District ("MRGCD") tracts—Tracts 4 through 7, 9 and 10 (as shown on MRGCD Maps 165 and 166)—and is situated west of BNSF's tracks and east of the Luis Lopez Community Ditch, south of the City of Socorro. A full legal description of the Brown Arroyo Property is attached hereto as Exhibit B.
   62│
   63│11. In the early to mid 1930s, the Middle Rio Grande Conservancy District ("MRGCD") acquired all of the tracts of land which comprise the Brown Arroyo Property, as well as other contiguous tracts of land adjacent to and west of the railroad tracks..
   64│
   65│12. All of the deeds into MRGCD by which it acquired the tracts lying west of the railroad tracks, including all the tracts which are now subsumed within the Brown Arroyo Property, recite that MRGCD acquired title to the land "for right-of-way for the Brown Arroyo control."
   66│
   67│13. By Easement dated September 23, 1936, ("1936 Easement") MRGCD granted to BNSF's predecessor, The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway Company, a right "to enter upon lands described in the easement and use so much of the natural material as such earth, rock, wood, etc. as it may elect or desire to remove for the purpose of constructing a surface ditch, dykes and spoil banks, together with any other facilities or structures necessary for the protection of the railroad or other [railroad] property from surface or other waters."
   68│
   69│14. In addition to such rights, the 1936 Easement grants BNSF a right of egress and ingress onto MRGCD Tracts 2-10 in Sections 19, 20 and 31 shown on District Map 165 and Tracts 1 and 8A in Section 31 on Map No. 166 "for the purpose of excavating, constructing and maintaining said ditch, dikes and spoil banks and shall be held harmless on account of any damages sustained to the land or crops hereafter grown thereon on account of said improvements." A copy of the 1936 Easement is attached hereto as Exhibit "A."
   70│
   71│15. The 1936 Easement further provides "that this right and easement shall be permanent and run with the lands, and be binding on the party of the first part [MRGCD] its successor and assigns."
   72│
   73│16. Defendant acquired its interest in the Brown Arroyo Property as part of larger purchase of land by deed filed in the Office of the County Clerk of Socorro County on December 29, 2003. The deed recites that property conveyed to Defendant is "subject to easements, rights of way reservations and restrictions."
   74│
   75│17. The 1936 Easement was recorded in the lands records of Socorro County on September 14, 1938. The tracts referenced in the Easement include the Brown Arroyo Property acquired by Defendant.
   76│
   77│18. The diversion system begins on BNSF property adjacent to its track where the original flow of the arroyo is diverted 90 degrees by a system of levees, dykes and channel that parallels the track. The system extends south off of BNSF's property, onto the Brown Arroyo Property, then onto other private land, and then back onto BNSF property where the channel elbows to the east and passes underneath BNSF's bridge at the railroad's milepost 981.3. The diversion system is approximately 2 miles in length.
   78│
   79│19. BNSF and its predecessors have historically maintained the diversion system, rebuilding the levees and dykes after breaches caused by floodwaters, entering upon the tracts referenced in the 1936 Easement.
   80│
   81│20. Between July 27, 2006 and August 6, 2006, unprecedented, extraordinary rainfall events caused extreme flooding throughout Socorro County.
   82│
   83│21. The extraordinary rainfall caused water flowing down the Brown Arroyo to breach the diversion levees in several locations and washed-out BNSF's track and roadbed.
   84│
   85│22. The breaches in the roadbed caused BNSF to cease operations for short-periods of time while the tracks and roadbeds were cleared and repaired.
   86│
   87│23. BNSF participated in meetings with federal and local officials to discuss short term and long term solution to repair flood damaged property and prevent future damage from storm water flooding. Soon after the breaches occurred, BNSF's contractors, in coordination with other task force members and at the considerable expense of BNSF, worked to rehabilitate the diversion system, clearing vegetation, building up the levees, expanding the diversion channel, and constructing piers to control floodwaters to minimize the likelihood of additional breaches and flood damage. Some of the rehabilitation work was done on the Brown Arroyo Property.
   88│
   89│24. In or about November 2006, Defendant notified BNSF of a claim that BNSF trespassed on the Brown Arroyo Property when rehabilitating the diversion system. Following such notice of Defendant's claim, the parties sought to resolve the dispute without resort to litigation.
   90│
   91│25. By email dated May 19, 2008, counsel for Defendant threatened that unless the matter is resolved by May 30, 2008, Defendant will mobilize earthmoving equipment and commence the removal of the diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property on June 3, 2008.
   92│
   93│26. In response to Defendant's threats, on June 3, 2008, BNSF filed this lawsuit seeking a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to prevent Defendant from destroying or interfering with the diversion system. On June 4, 2008, this Court entered a temporary restraining order restraining Defendant's threatened conduct which expires by its own terms.
   94│
   95│27. Since the expiration of the temporary restraining order, although Defendant has not removed and/or destroyed the work on the diversion system as originally threatened, it has placed what appear to be survey stakes on a portion of the dike located on the Brown Arroyo
   96│
   97│Property. Defendant has further refused to recognize the validity of the 1936 Easement and has indicated an intention to perform work which would damage or impede the Brown Arroyo diversion system.
   98│
   99│28. Removal, interference with, or modification of the diversion system, the purpose of which is to control the high volume of floodwaters of the Brown Arroyo to prevent damage to the railroad and other property, will likely result in the wash out of BNSF's tracks, the flooding of adjacent landowners' property and will significantly interfere with the interstate railroad system.
  100│
  101│## **FIRST CLAIM FOR RELIEF** (Declaratory Judgment – Express Grant of Easement)
  102│
  103│29. BNSF incorporates by reference as though fully set forth herein paragraphs 1 through 28 of its Complaint.
  104│
  105│30. BNSF is the holder of an express easement, recorded in the land records of Socorro County, which allows it the right of egress and ingress onto the Brown Arroyo Property, and the right to use of natural materials on the Brown Arroyo Property to construct and maintain the diversion system.
  106│
  107│31. Under the terms if the 1936 Easement BNSF had the right to enter the Brown Arroyo Property and rehabilitate the Brown Arroyo diversion system to prevent further damage to railroad property and that of adjacent landowners.
  108│
  109│32. By law, Defendant had notice of the grant of easement and any interest owned by Defendant in a tract or the Brown Arroyo Property is subject to and subservient to BNSF's rights under the 1936 Easement.
  110│
  111│33. An actual and justifiable controversy has arisen and now exists between BNSF and Defendant concerning BNSF's right to enter and use the Brown Arroyo Property for the
  112│
  113│construction and maintenance of the diversion system. BNSF is entitled to judicial declaration by this court pursuant to the New Mexico Declaratory Judgment Act, NMSA 1978, §§ 44-6-1 to 44-6-15 and Rule 1-057 NMRA that BNSF is the holder of an express easement on the Brown Arroyo Property for the use of constructing and maintaining a diversion system to control floodwaters flowing down the Brown Arroyo.
  114│
  115│## **SECOND CLAIM FOR RELIEF**
  116│
  117│(Declaratory Judgment – Implied Easement by Necessity or Estoppel)
  118│
  119│34. BNSF incorporates by reference as though fully set forth herein paragraphs 1 through 33 of its Complaint.
  120│
  121│35. Alternatively, if BNSF does not have an express grant of easement, or if BNSF does not have the right of egress and ingress over the Brown Arroyo Property to continue to maintain the Brown Arroyo Diversion system as was done in 2006, BNSF has an easement by necessity or estoppel.
  122│
  123│36. The tracts of land on which the diversion system is located, including the tracts which comprise the Brown Arroyo Property, are contiguous and were previously owned by MRGCD, which acquired the tracts for the express purpose of Brown Arroyo flood control.
  124│
  125│37. Severance of the Brown Arroyo Property and the land now owned by BNSF curtailed access of BNSF to and from the diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property.
  126│
  127│38. A reasonable necessity existed for the diversion system at the time the BNSF land and the Brown Arroyo Property were severed which continues today.
  128│
  129│39. The Brown Arroyo diversion system has been located on the Brown Arroyo Property, and maintained by the railroad, whether BNSF or its predecessor AT&SF, with the knowledge of, and without objection from, Defendant's predecessors in interest for approximately 70 years.
  130│
  131│40. An actual and justiciable controversy has arisen and now exists between BNSF and Defendant concerning BNSF's right to enter and use the Brown Arroyo Property for the construction and maintenance of the diversion system. BNSF is entitled to judicial declaration by this court pursuant to the New Mexico Declaratory Judgment Act, NMSA 1978, §§ 44-6-1 to 44-6-15 and Rule 1-057 NMRA that BNSF is the holder of an implied easement by necessity or estoppel on the Brown Arroyo Property for the use of constructing and maintaining a diversion system to control floodwaters flowing down the Brown Arroyo.
  132│
  133│## **THIRD CLAIM FOR RELIEF** (Injunction)
  134│
  135│41. BNSF incorporates by reference as though fully set forth herein paragraphs 1 through 38 of the Complaint.
  136│
  137│42. Defendant's threatened conduct of destroying the diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property will expose BNSF's property and operations as well as other landowners' property to a significant risk of injury from floodwaters flowing down the Brown Arroyo.
  138│
  139│43. The dikes, levees and channel comprising the Brown Arroyo diversion system are part of BNSF's railroad facilities. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1992, it is crime to undermine any tunnel, bridge, viaduct, trestle, track, signal, station, depot, warehouse, terminal, or any other way, structure, property, or appurtenance used in the operation of any such railroad in interstate or foreign commerce. The conduct threatened by Defendant will result in a breach of the peace and violation of this statute.
  140│
  141│44. Unless Defendant's threatened conduct as described herein is enjoined, BNSF will suffer irreparable injury and harm for which there is no adequate remedy at law.
  142│
  143│45. The equity and hardships between BNSF and Defendant support issuance of a permanent injunction prohibiting Defendant from removing, interfering with, or modifying the diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property.
  144│
  145│46. BNSF seeks to maintain the *status quo* with respect to the diversion system which has been located on the Brown Arroyo Property for approximately 70 years.
  146│
  147│47. The Court should enter an injunction prohibiting Defendant, its agents, servants, employees and attorneys from removing, interfering with, or modifying the floodwater diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property and from interfering with any efforts of BNSF or its agents or contractors to maintain the floodwater diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property in the future.
  148│
  149│WHEREFORE, BNSF respectfully requests the Court to award the following relief:
  150│
  151│A. Declare that BNSF that the 1936 Easement is valid and binding on Defendant and entitles BNSF to enter upon the Brown Arroyo Property to conduct and maintain the Brown Arroyo diversion system, including the work performed by BNSF's contractor in the summer of 2006.
  152│
  153│B. Enter a permanent injunction restraining Defendant Roy Mercer, L.L.C. and its agents, servants, employees and attorneys from removing, interfering with, or modifying the floodwater diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property and from interfering with the efforts of BNSF or its agents or contractors to maintain the floodwater diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property in the future.
  154│
  155│C. In the event Defendant attempts to remove, destroy or alter any part of the work performed to rehabilitate the Brown Arroyo diversion system during the pendency of this case, enter a preliminary injunction prohibiting Defendant and its agents, servants, employees and
  156│
  157│attorneys from removing, interfering with, or modifying the floodwater diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property and from interfering with the efforts of BNSF or its agents or contractors to maintain the floodwater diversion system on the Brown Arroyo Property.
  158│
  159│- D. Recovery of prejudgment and post-judgment interest on any amounts due BNSF.
  160│- E. Recovery of BNSF's costs of suit.
  161│- F. Such other and further relief this Court deems just and proper.
  162│
  163│MODRALL, SPERLING, ROEHL, HARRIS  
  164│& SISK, P.A.

Answer three things about the file above.

1. Does it contain an instrument, as defined? If not, return an empty
   `instrument_name` and say in `note` what the document is instead. If it does,
   name it and give the first and last line of the instrument itself — cutting
   off any filing that wraps it and any unrelated exhibit that follows.

2. Is this file one part of a document split across several files? The other
   files in the same bundle are listed above with their opening and closing
   words. If the instrument in this file begins part-way through a document
   whose earlier part is one of those files, give that file's name in
   `continues_from`; otherwise return an empty string. If this file's text
   breaks off mid-document rather than ending properly, set `ends_mid_document`
   to true.

3. List every substantive provision of the instrument, in document order. For
   each: a short name including its number if it has one; the first and last
   line it occupies; its text, repaired as described; and one sentence in
   `repairs` saying what you fixed, or an empty string if nothing needed fixing.

A line may hold more than one provision — the OCR often runs lettered
sub-provisions together on a single line. When that happens, give each
sub-provision the same line range and let the text tell them apart.
